papers.title: Longitudinal Multi-Dimensional Analysis of India-Pakistan Conflict Discourse on Reddit (2019-2025)
papers.abstract: Six India--Pakistan crises between 2019 and 2025, from the Pulwama attack to Operation Sindoor, have each been argued out on Reddit in India-aligned communities such as \texttt{r/india}, in Pakistan-aligned communities such as \texttt{r/pakistan}, and in general-audience ones such as \texttt{r/worldnews}. A strike can be a security issue in one community and a question of who was harmed in another. Computational studies of the conflict have concentrated on the February 2019 crisis, with some splitting posts by national side, but to the best of our knowledge none has compared how differently aligned communities frame a series of crises. To investigate this, we collected 43K posts from ten such communities on Reddit and, after filtering, used a mixed-methods approach to analyze the 305K comments under the relevant posts. We label each comment's narrative frame with GPT-5.2 and measure contestation with Reddit's flag for comments that draw many votes in both directions. Contestation rates differ 2.5-fold between general-audience and India-aligned communities and 1.8-fold between humanitarian and economic framing, but only 1.1-fold between comments that Perspective scores as toxic and the rest. The mix of frames and sentiment tracks the kind of crisis more closely than its year: the first and last crises, both military and six years apart, draw nearly identical mixes, and the 2019 revocation of Article 370 draws a different one. Crossing into another group of communities sharpens opposition rather than softening it: commenters who post both inside and outside their usual group oppose the other side more often outside it, even as slightly fewer of their comments attack a person or group.

papers.title: DLS: Dual-Logic Graph Neural Networks with Chaos-Fuzzy Residuals for Robust Link Prediction
papers.abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph mining, critical for applications ranging from biological interaction discovery to recommender systems. While Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art results, they are fundamentally limited by the inadvertent suppression of high-frequency signals, as the recursive aggregation that stabilizes structural learning inherently leads to over-smoothing, rendering node representations indistinguishable in deep layers. This limitation is particularly severe in heterophilous graphs, where structural proximity does not imply feature similarity. In this paper, we propose DLS (Dual-Logic SAGE), a novel inductive framework designed to break the over-smoothing barrier via a "controlled instability" mechanism. Unlike conventional methods relying on static structural heuristics, DLS introduces a dynamic residual pipeline. First, a Chaotic Injection Module utilizes the Logistic Map to diversify the feature manifold, exploiting sensitivity to initial conditions to separate topologically similar but semantically distinct nodes. Second, to mitigate the aleatoric uncertainty introduced by chaotic dynamics, a Fuzzy-Logic Gating Mechanism applies soft-thresholding to filter noise and retain only high-confidence signals. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DLS effectively balances feature discrimination with robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in heterophilous settings while maintaining competitive efficiency on standard homophilous graphs.

papers.title: Cycles of Arbitrary Period in Multidimensional Heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause Dynamics
papers.abstract: We study periodic behavior in heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause opinion dynamics with multidimensional opinions and norm-defined confidence neighborhoods. We prove that, for every dimension $d\ge3$, every $\ell_q$ norm with $q\in[1,\infty]\setminus\{2\}$, and every integer $m\ge2$, a system of five agents admits a periodic trajectory of minimal period $m$; moreover, different periods can coexist for fixed confidence radii. Four agents remain stationary, while the fifth moves along a line segment contained in their convex hull. The stationary agents may share a common strictly positive confidence radius, and all confidence inequalities are strict. A geometric criterion underlying the construction extends these results to further classes of norms. However, this criterion cannot be satisfied in dimensions one and two, regardless of the confidence norm. We also prove that no heterogeneous Hegselmann-Krause system with less than five agents admits a nonconstant periodic trajectory, under any norm and in any dimension; every trajectory with at most three agents converges exponentially.

papers.title: Manufactured Authenticity: How Behavioral Signals Are Produced and Misread in Online Markets
papers.abstract: Online platforms increasingly ask users to infer credibility from behavioral signals whose production conditions are opaque. We introduce manufactured authenticity: the platform-mediated production of observable activity that interfaces invite users to read as organic participation. Using 996,834 cryptocurrency tokens and 50,895 creator wallets from Pump.fun, a Solana-based token launchpad, we examine how legitimacy signals are produced in an automation-enabled online market. We identify four production strategies (high-velocity launching, passive launching, template-content creation, and organic-style creation) that generate distinct but interface-similar cues of activity, narrative plausibility, and participation. High-velocity and template-content strategies emerge as alternatives rather than cumulative layers: the former produces activity at scale, while the latter produces descriptions associated with higher reply engagement. Yet visible engagement does not imply broader diffusion: template-like content attracts replies without greater ownership dispersion, and tokens associated with non-organic production strategies exhibit more concentrated investor holdings than organic-style tokens. We argue that platform governance should move beyond detecting manipulation toward making signal provenance legible. We propose authenticity disclosure as a design approach for surfacing production conditions without requiring definitive claims about automation, AI authorship, or actor intent.

papers.title: Spatial Price Formation in Transport Networks: A Variational Approach
papers.abstract: This paper formulates a model of spatial price formation in a closed regional economy, with finitely many production nodes and finitely many demand nodes embedded in a continuous geographic domain. Transportation costs depend on the geometry of the region and on an underlying network of feasible connections. Prices are modeled as a spatial field constrained by arbitrage and transport feasibility. The equilibrium price system is characterized by a variational problem. A second minimization selects an equilibrium-compatible price field with minimum spatial energy and permits the use of Euler--Lagrange methods. The framework clarifies what observed prices and quantities reveal about demand, and uses known transport costs to bound unobserved prices and exclude directed arcs from equilibrium shipments. A five-node example illustrates equilibrium, alternative shipment patterns, and the information supplied by partial price observations. We give a numerical procedure for planar domains and outline an extension to spherical domains.

papers.title: High-Coverage Blind Spots in Online Abuse Monitoring: Account Selection, Held-Out Flagging Rates, and Sample Composition
papers.abstract: Platforms with limited monitoring capacity may rank target accounts by the number of abusive replies received or by the share of replies labeled abusive. We test how these rankings affect account selection, historical flagged-reply coverage, and held-out labeling rates. In the Online Abusive Attacks (OAA) data (945,987 replies to 384 accounts), two 25-account lists share just one account. Count-based selection covers 75.56% of flagged replies, while rate-based selection covers 5.04%. In a 500-iteration stratified historical hold-out, the lists have labeling rates of 2.69% and 4.98%, respectively (1.85 times). A volume- and group-preserving null model produces low list overlap without a corresponding rate advantage. We repeat the comparison on a second dataset of replies to UK election candidates. The two 25-account lists overlap in eight accounts, but the rate advantage is smaller in historical splits and reverses in three matched-group chronological tests. The findings distinguish differences in who is selected for monitoring from differences in future labeling rates across populations and time.

papers.title: Inferring Locations and Correcting Bias in Infectious Disease Data Using Human Mobility
papers.abstract: Understanding and reconstructing infectious disease transmission remains challenging due to sparsely sampled and biased epidemiological case data: only a small fraction of infectious disease cases are reported to health authorities, and an even smaller fraction are sent to labs for genomic sequencing. In this work, we study the problem of inferring unobserved transmission events by integrating pathogen genomic data with human mobility information. Intuitively, even if we do not have case data for a certain region, such as a census block group, we can use massive-scale individual mobility data to understand where people may be exposed and infer where unobserved cases may be located. Assuming only a subset of cases are reported and sequenced, we reconstruct a phylogenetic tree from observed cases and transform it into a partial transmission tree using the outbreaker2 tool. This tree contains inferred transmissions based on the genetic distance of the observed cases. As these inferred nodes have unknown locations, we propose a mobility-aware belief propagation approach to estimate their locations using human mobility data. Experiments on simulated and real-world genomic surveillance data with biased sampling show that incorporating mobility data improves the reconstruction of inferred transmission trees, reducing cross-entropy relative to the observed distribution by 39.4% and 16.1%, respectively. Results on real-world COVID-19 sequence data show the promise of combining genomic and mobility data for more reliable location inference, with potential implications for outbreak analysis and public health decision-making.

papers.title: Finding Patient Zero in Temporal Contact Networks: A Comparative Study
papers.abstract: Identifying the source of an epidemic, i.e., the patient zero, in a temporal contact network is important for effective outbreak containment and resource allocation. While several methods have been proposed for this task, they have rarely been evaluated under comparable conditions, and no systematic comparison exists for temporal contact networks. We address this gap with a comparative study of seven major methods, namely Steiner Tree (ST), Individual-Based Approximation (IBA), Dynamic Message Passing (DMP), Monte Carlo Mean-Field (MCMF), Soft Margin Estimator (SME), Backtracking Network (BN, a graph neural network), and Belief Propagation (BP). We unify all methods under a single problem formulation and evaluate them on eight diverse temporal networks. In the main experiment, we compare source detection performance for varying basic reproduction numbers. Three complementary experiments on a subset of networks study (i) learning curves, (ii) partial observability, and (iii) parameter misspecification. We find that BP and BN are the strongest source detectors overall. SME is strong under partial observation but mediocre otherwise. IBA, DMP, and MCMF share a common weakness rooted in their factorized-likelihood assumption, leading to overconfident predictions. We identify scaling these methods to larger networks as the most pressing direction for future work.

papers.title: A comparative exploration of Steinerberger curvature and resistance curvature in model and real-world complex networks
papers.abstract: Discrete curvature extends the concept of curvature from continuous spaces to discrete structures such as graphs and networks. It provides a mathematical framework for characterising local and global network geometry, that offers insights into structural properties such as connectivity and clustering. In this study, we investigate Steinerberger curvature (SBC) and resistance curvature (RC) and examine their relationships with established graph curvature measures, namely Forman-Ricci, Augmented Forman-Ricci, and Ollivier-Ricci curvatures, a notion of scalar sectional curvature, as well as conventional vertex-based measures. A systematic comparative analysis is conducted across various synthetic network models and real-world networks, focusing on curvature distributions, correlations with structural measures, and the identification of structurally important vertices through network disintegration experiments based on global efficiency. Our results show that SBC generally exhibits weaker correlations with other measures. On the other hand, RC is strongly positively correlated with established discrete Ricci curvature measures, whereas it is predominantly negatively correlated with conventional vertex-based measures like degree and centrality-based measures. Furthermore, RC achieves a reduction in communication efficiency comparable to or faster than established Ricci curvature measures. These findings suggest that SBC captures structural characteristics that are largely distinct from those reflected by other measures, while RC exhibits distinct structural associations and shows significant potential for identifying vertices critical to network connectivity.

papers.title: Shortest-path percolation and structural robustness of quantum internet networks
papers.abstract: We study shortest-path percolation on spatial networks that model the quantum internet based on optical fibers. In this process, the removal of paths describes the consumption of the entangled links used for communication. We compare finite and unrestricted path-length bounds for networks whose average degree either increases with system size or remains approximately constant. We show that networks become more robust as the average degree increases, whereas networks with approximately constant average degree exhibit a data collapse for the fixed finite bounds considered. Using Monte Carlo sampling of the shortest-path-length distribution, we estimate an equivalent path cost, a finite bound that approximately reproduces the degradation of the network in the unrestricted case. For networks with fixed average degree, this cost grows approximately as the square root of the number of nodes. Increasing the bound beyond this value requires additional computation time without appreciably changing the percolation dynamics. As a complementary result, for Erd\H{o}s-R\'enyi random networks, we find an empirical relation between the initial average degree and the approximately common crossing point of the percolation curves for different path-length bounds.

papers.title: Asymmetric Discourse Homogenization on Reddit Was a Text-Length Artifact: A Reanalysis
papers.abstract: In the first version of this paper I reported that conservative Reddit users began writing more alike after ChatGPT was released while progressive users did not. That result came from a similarity measure that rises and falls with comment length. I redo every analysis of the original paper on all 6,056,593 comments with a sentence encoder and a dispersion measure computed within length strata, and the conservative break goes away. The two camps show no reliable difference in how within-group similarity changed after late 2022, and the ChatGPT date behaves like any of the more than two thousand other cutoffs I test. The matched flair comparison, the cumulative AI index, the stayer panel and the entropy signature each lose their support once length is held fixed. The one change that survives is older. Left and right comments drew closer to each other between 2019 and 2022, and that convergence was complete before ChatGPT arrived. I end with what this implies for studies that measure homogenization with embeddings.

papers.title: Network sampling: a comparative review
papers.abstract: Network sampling is essential for the study of real world systems, since access to the topological structure and dynamical characteristics of a complex system is usually infeasible, and can also prove computationally intractable for large and dense networks. However, the field still lacks systematic methodologies that allow a procedural analysis of sampling plans for connected data. Hence, this study aims to compare network sampling methods through the usage of multivariate statistical analysis and machine learning techniques that are anchored in network metrics' estimation of synthetic and real-world networks. It was demonstrated that no single sampling strategy dominates both cases, although Forest fire and Frontier sampling have presented the most consistent performance across all topologies investigated. The impact of each structural property of these networks for principal component analysis and classification results were also discussed, with consistent pattern groups seen for both data types. Transfer learning aimed at real-world network identification has also demonstrated that realistic structural connections can be correlated to well-known network models through the usage of sampled subgraphs' properties for model training, providing an avenue to real-world network characterization through sampling methodologies.
